title: Lena's week
text: My name is Lena. I am twenty years old, and I live with my parents in a small town. From Monday to Friday, I work in a café. I start at seven in the morning and finish at three in the afternoon. I like my job because I meet a lot of people. On Saturdays, I visit my grandmother. She lives near the sea, and we often walk on the beach together. On Sundays, I stay at home and read.

title: A message from Ella
text:
Hi Sam,
Thanks for your message. I'm sorry, but I can't come to your party on Saturday. My cousin is getting married that day, and the whole family is going to the wedding in another city. We're leaving on Friday evening and coming back on Sunday afternoon. Can we meet next week instead? I'm free on Tuesday after work. We could try the new Italian restaurant near the station. I've heard it's very good. Let me know!
Best wishes,
Ella

title: A new way to work
text: When Daniel's company moved to a new building on the other side of the city, he was worried that getting to work would become much harder. The bus took fifty minutes, and he often had to stand all the way. After two weeks, a colleague suggested cycling. Daniel was not sure at first: he had not ridden a bike for years, and the main road looked dangerous. Then he discovered a quiet route along the river that was only a little longer. Now he cycles to work four days a week. He arrives earlier than before, feels less tired in the afternoons, and says he has even started to enjoy rainy days.

title: Gardens between buildings
text: In many cities, empty land between buildings is being turned into community gardens. Supporters say the benefits go well beyond fresh vegetables. Residents who previously only nodded to each other in the street now share tools, swap advice and plan weekend events together. Researchers studying one such project found that people reported feeling safer and less isolated after its first year. Critics, however, point out that gardens rarely survive without a small group of hard-working volunteers, and when those people move away, the plots are often abandoned within months. The most successful projects, it seems, are those that train new members to take on responsibility from the start, rather than depending on the few enthusiastic people who started them.

title: What gets counted
text: Productivity is often measured by what can be counted: emails answered, tasks closed, hours logged. The appeal is obvious. Numbers are easy to compare and seem to remove personal bias from decisions about pay and promotion. Yet the most valuable work in many companies resists this kind of measurement. An engineer who spends a week rethinking a design may produce nothing visible, and then prevent months of costly errors. A manager who calmly settles a conflict leaves no record at all. When only countable output is rewarded, people sensibly shift their effort to it, and the harder, slower work of thinking is quietly squeezed out. The danger is not that the numbers are false, but that they are partial, and that we forget this.

title: The edited past
text: It is tempting to treat nostalgia as a harmless indulgence, a warm bath of memory into which we sink when the present disappoints. Psychologists have lately offered a more flattering account: recalling cherished moments, they argue, can strengthen a sense of meaning and connection, particularly in times of upheaval. Yet the comfort nostalgia provides is curiously selective. The past it serves up has been edited, its tedium and anxieties trimmed away, so that what we long for is less a period we actually lived through than a version of it we have quietly composed. This need not make nostalgia dishonest, merely creative. The risk arises only when that composition is mistaken for a record and offered as a blueprint for how the future ought to look.

title: Library notice
text: From next month, the city library will open on Sundays for the first time. The new hours, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., are a response to a survey in which many people said they could not visit during the week because of work. To pay for the extra day, the library will close one hour earlier on Wednesdays. Members can still return books at any time using the box by the main door. The library also plans to start a reading club for teenagers later in the year. Anyone who would like to help run the club should speak to a member of staff or send an email before the end of this month.

title: Learning by teaching
text: Teachers often joke that they only truly understood their subject once they had to explain it to others. Research suggests there is some truth in this. In several studies, students who were told they would later teach the material to classmates remembered more of it than students who expected only to take a test, even though neither group actually taught anyone. The expectation alone seemed to change how they studied: they arranged ideas more carefully and looked for links between them rather than learning isolated facts by heart. The effect has limits, however. When the material was very difficult, the pressure of having to explain it appeared to make some students anxious, and the advantage disappeared.

title: My friend Maria
text: This is my friend Maria. She is from Brazil, but now she lives in Rome with her husband and two children. Maria is a nurse. She works at a big hospital in the city. Her husband, Paolo, is a cook in a small restaurant. They have a dog called Bruno. On Sundays, the family goes to the park. The children play football, and Maria and Paolo walk with Bruno.

title: City Bikes
text: CITY BIKES – see the city on two wheels! You can rent a bike for one hour, half a day or a whole day. One hour costs 5 euros, and a whole day costs 20 euros. Children under 12 must wear a helmet, and we give helmets free to everyone. We are open every day from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., but in winter we close at 5 p.m. Please bring your ID card when you rent a bike.

title: A home for lost animals
text: Last summer, Mia started working as a volunteer at a home for lost dogs and cats near where she lived. She had always loved animals, but pets were not allowed in her building, so this seemed like the perfect solution. At first, her jobs were simple: cleaning cages and filling water bowls. After a month, the staff trusted her to walk the dogs and to help visitors who wanted to take an animal home. Mia says the hardest part is saying goodbye when a dog she has looked after goes to a new family. Still, she thinks it is also the best part, because it means the animal finally has a home.

title: Parking and local shops
text: Shop owners often fight plans to remove parking spaces from busy streets, fearing that customers will disappear. The evidence, however, tells a more complicated story. Several studies have found that shop owners tend to overestimate how many of their customers arrive by car, sometimes by a factor of two. People who walk or cycle may spend less on each visit, but they usually come back more often, and over a month they can spend as much as drivers or more. That does not mean every street benefits. Where public transport is poor, removing parking can genuinely hurt local businesses. The lesson seems to be that such decisions should be based on local data rather than on assumptions.

title: What translation apps cannot carry
text: Free translation apps have become so accurate that some people now question whether learning a foreign language is worth the effort. The argument has a certain logic: if a phone can handle a menu or a business email, why spend years mastering grammar? Yet this view rests on a narrow idea of what language is for. Translation tools are designed to transfer information, and they do that remarkably well. What they cannot easily transfer is the trust that grows when someone makes the effort to speak your language, however imperfectly. Negotiators, doctors and teachers all report that a few sentences in a person's own language can change the tone of an entire conversation. In that sense, the apps may make language learning less necessary for transactions, but no less valuable for relationships.

title: The illusion of understanding
text: Ask people whether they understand how a lock, a toilet or a bicycle works, and most will say yes with confidence. Ask them to explain it step by step, and that confidence tends to collapse. Psychologists call this gap the illusion of explanatory depth. It persists, they suggest, because everyday familiarity masquerades as comprehension: we have used these objects so often that their workings feel known. The illusion is largely harmless when it concerns household devices. It becomes more consequential when it extends to policy, where people often hold firm views on matters whose mechanisms they could not begin to describe. Intriguingly, asking people to explain a policy in detail, rather than to justify their position, tends to moderate their views, not because they are persuaded, but because they discover how little they knew.
